stem: Driftlight wants the plan tiers to appear cheapest to priciest in every chart, whatever the minutes watched. Which sort fits?

options.text: A computed sort by `SUM(Minutes Watched)`, descending
options.rationale: This orders plans by minutes, so the tiers would follow viewing, not price.

options.text: An alphabetic sort, ascending
options.rationale: Alphabetical order puts Basic, Basic with Ads, Premium, Standard, which is not the price order.

options.text: A manual sort, by dragging the headers or choosing Manual in the Sort dialog
options.rationale: A manual order is fixed, so it keeps the price order even when the data changes.

options.text: A computed sort by `Plan` using the Data Source Order option
options.rationale: Data source order depends on how the data happens to be stored, not on price, and gives no deliberate tier order.

explanation: A computed sort follows a value and reorders when the data changes. A natural order such as plan tiers has to be fixed by hand, which is what a manual sort does.

stem: A bar chart shows `SUM(Minutes Watched)` by Genre. After every data refresh the longest bar must be first. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Sort Genre by the field `Minutes Watched` with a Sum aggregation, descending
options.rationale: A sort by a field is computed, so it re-sorts whenever the values change.

options.text: Drag the Genre headers into the right order by hand
options.rationale: Dragging headers makes a manual sort, which stays put when the totals change.

options.text: Choose Manual in the Sort dialog and move the genres up and down
options.rationale: Manual is a fixed order and will not follow the data after a refresh.

options.text: Sort Genre alphabetically, descending
options.rationale: Alphabetical order ignores the minutes, so the longest bar may land anywhere.

explanation: "Always biggest first" calls for a computed sort. Use a sort icon, the toolbar buttons or Sort > Field, and the order updates with the data.

stem: In the Sort dialog, which Sort By option orders members by an aggregated value of a measure, such as a sum?

options.text: Alphabetic
options.rationale: This sorts members by their names, not by any measure.

options.text: Manual
options.rationale: This lets you place members yourself and ignores values.

options.text: Data Source Order
options.rationale: This keeps the order in which members appear in the data source.

options.text: Field
options.rationale: Field is "the field value used to determine the sort order", with an aggregation such as Sum.

explanation: The Sort By options are Data Source Order, Alphabetic, Field, Manual and Nested. Only Field computes the order from a value such as `SUM(Minutes Watched)`.

stem: An analyst clicks the sort icon on the Genre header once. How are the genres ordered?

options.text: Ascending by the measure in the view
options.rationale: Ascending needs a second click.

options.text: Descending by the measure in the view
options.rationale: One click sorts descending; a second click sorts ascending and a third clears the sort.

options.text: Alphabetically from A to Z
options.rationale: The icon sorts by the measure in the view, not by member names.

options.text: Back in data source order
options.rationale: The original order only returns after the sort is cleared with a third click.

explanation: The sort icons give a computed sort: one click descending, two clicks ascending, three clicks clear it.

stem: A view has one pane per Region, each showing Genre bars. The analyst sorts by clicking the sort icon on the measure axis. What kind of sort results by default?

options.text: A manual sort that applies the same order to every pane
options.rationale: Manual sorts come from dragging headers or the Manual option, not from an axis icon.

options.text: An alphabetical sort of the genres
options.rationale: An axis sort orders by the measure, not by names.

options.text: A nested sort, which orders the genres within each pane
options.rationale: Sorting from an axis gives a nested sort by default.

options.text: A sort of the panes themselves by their totals
options.rationale: The axis sort orders members inside each pane, not the panes.

explanation: Sorting from an axis sorts within each pane, while sorting from a field label does not nest. That is why panes can show different orders.

stem: Which two actions create a manual sort of the Plan headers? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Click the sort icon on the measure axis
options.rationale: This creates a computed sort by the measure.

options.text: Select a Plan header in the view and drag it to a new position
options.rationale: Dragging a header fixes the order by hand.

options.text: Choose Sort > Field with a Sum aggregation
options.rationale: Field is a computed sort that follows the values.

options.text: Choose Manual in the Sort dialog and move the plans up or down
options.rationale: Manual lets you set the order member by member.

options.text: Click the descending sort button on the toolbar
options.rationale: The toolbar buttons give a computed sort.

explanation: A manual sort is fixed by hand and does not react to the data. Computed sorts use a measure and re-sort when values change.

stem: Which two ways remove a sort that is applied to a field? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Right-click the field and choose Clear Sort
options.rationale: This removes the sort from that field.

options.text: Click the sort icon once
options.rationale: One click sorts descending; it does not clear.

options.text: Choose Clear Sorts from the toolbar's clear sheet menu
options.rationale: This clears every sort on the sheet.

options.text: Choose Alphabetic in the Sort dialog
options.rationale: This applies an alphabetic sort rather than clearing.

options.text: Click the line and select Remove
options.rationale: That removes a reference line, not a sort.

explanation: Clear Sort works on one field and Clear Sorts on the whole sheet. Clicking a sort icon three times also clears a computed sort.

stem: The content team set a fixed target of 120 hours per genre. Which reference line value should the analyst use?

options.text: Constant
options.rationale: A constant draws the line at a number you enter, such as a target.

options.text: Average
options.rationale: Average draws the mean of the marks, which moves with the data.

options.text: Median
options.rationale: Median draws the middle value of the marks, not a fixed target.

options.text: Total
options.rationale: Total draws the sum of the marks, not a fixed target.

explanation: A reference line value is either a Constant or a computation over the marks: Total, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Average or Median. A target is a fixed number, so use Constant.

stem: A view has one pane per Region, each showing Genre bars. The analyst wants a separate average line in every Region's pane. Which scope should be set?

options.text: Table
options.rationale: Table scope draws a single line across the whole table.

options.text: Pane
options.rationale: Pane scope draws one line per pane.

options.text: Cell
options.rationale: Cell scope draws one line per cell, which here would mean one per bar.

options.text: Total
options.rationale: Total is a computation that sums the marks, not a scope.

explanation: Table, Pane and Cell define the scope of a reference line: one line for the whole table, one per pane, or one per cell.

stem: How can an analyst add a reference line directly from a view, without using the Analytics pane?

options.text: Right-click a discrete header and select Add Reference Line
options.rationale: A discrete header has no continuous scale to draw a line on.

options.text: Right-click the Marks card and select Add Reference Line
options.rationale: The Marks card holds mark properties, not reference lines.

options.text: Double-click the title of the worksheet
options.rationale: The title is for text and does not open the reference line dialog.

options.text: Right-click a quantitative axis and select Add Reference Line
options.rationale: Reference lines attach to a quantitative axis.

explanation: You can drag Reference Line from the Analytics pane onto the view, or right-click a quantitative axis and select Add Reference Line.

stem: An analyst wants to shade the area behind the marks between two constant values, 100 and 200. Which item should be added?

options.text: A reference band
options.rationale: Reference bands shade an area behind the marks between two constant or computed values.

options.text: A reference line
options.rationale: A line marks one value, not an area between two.

options.text: A box plot
options.rationale: A box plot shows quartiles and whiskers, not a band between chosen values.

options.text: A grand total
options.rationale: Totals add summed values to the table, not shading.

explanation: Reference lines, bands, distributions and box plots are built from the same dialog. A band is the one that shades between two values.

stem: The head of content wants to type a target of their own and see the line move. What should the reference line use for its value?

options.text: The Median computation
options.rationale: Median is recomputed from the data and cannot be typed in.

options.text: Cell scope
options.rationale: Scope controls where the lines are drawn, not where the value comes from.

options.text: A parameter
options.rationale: A parameter holds a single value the viewer can change, and a reference line can use it.

options.text: The Total computation
options.rationale: Total sums the marks, so it ignores anything typed.

explanation: A parameter is a workbook variable that can replace a constant in a calculation, filter or reference line. It lets a viewer supply the target.

stem: Which two are computations a reference line can use for its value? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Average
options.rationale: Average is offered, along with Total, Sum, Minimum, Maximum and Median.

options.text: Rank
options.rationale: Rank is a quick table calculation, not a reference line computation.

options.text: Running total
options.rationale: Running total is a quick table calculation.

options.text: Median
options.rationale: Median is one of the computations.

options.text: Percent of total
options.rationale: This is a quick table calculation.

explanation: A reference line value is a Constant or a computation over the marks. Rank, running total and percent of total belong to quick table calculations.

stem: The Add Reference Line dialog also builds related items. Which three can it create? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Reference bands
options.rationale: Bands shade an area between two values.

options.text: Histograms
options.rationale: Histograms come from bins or Show Me.

options.text: Distributions
options.rationale: Distributions use percentages, percentiles, quantiles or standard deviations.

options.text: Quick table calculations
options.rationale: These are applied from a measure pill's menu.

options.text: Box plots
options.rationale: Box plots add quartiles and whiskers to a continuous axis.

explanation: The reference line dialog also makes bands, distributions and box plots, all drawn on a continuous axis.

stem: A line chart shows monthly `SUM(Minutes Watched)`. Which quick table calculation shows viewing building up over the year?

options.text: Difference
options.rationale: Difference shows the change from the previous month, not the accumulated total.

options.text: Percent of total
options.rationale: Percent of total shows each month as a share of the whole.

options.text: Moving average
options.rationale: Moving average smooths values over a window and does not accumulate.

options.text: Running total
options.rationale: Running total adds each month to the sum of the months before it.

explanation: Running total is cumulative. Difference, percent of total and moving average answer different questions: change, share and smoothing.

stem: Where does an analyst apply a quick table calculation such as Rank to a measure?

options.text: Right-click the measure in the Data pane and choose Create > Quick Table Calculation
options.rationale: The Data pane's Create menu offers bins, not table calculations.

options.text: Right-click the measure pill in the view and choose Quick Table Calculation
options.rationale: Quick table calculations live on the pill's menu.

options.text: Drag Rank from the Analytics pane onto the view
options.rationale: The Analytics pane holds items such as Reference Line and Totals.

options.text: Select Analysis > Create Calculated Field and pick Rank
options.rationale: That builds a new calculated field from a formula.

explanation: Right-click a measure pill in the view, choose Quick Table Calculation and then a type such as Running total, Percent of total or Rank.

stem: Which sign tells you a quick table calculation is applied to a pill?

options.text: A delta symbol on the field
options.rationale: Tableau puts a delta symbol on the field.

options.text: An equal sign next to the field name in the Data pane
options.rationale: That marks calculated fields.

options.text: The suffix (bin) in the field name
options.rationale: That marks a field created with Create > Bins.

options.text: A green background on the pill
options.rationale: Green only says the pill is continuous.

explanation: A delta shows a table calculation. A calculated field has an equal sign in the Data pane, and a binned field has (bin) in its name.

stem: A rank table calculation counts marks in the wrong direction. Where can the analyst change how it is computed?

options.text: Right-click the field in the Data pane and choose Edit
options.rationale: That edits a calculated field's formula, and a quick table calculation is not one.

options.text: Click the sort icon on the axis
options.rationale: Sorting changes the order of marks, not how the calculation runs.

options.text: Right-click the pill and choose Edit Table Calculation
options.rationale: There the calculation type and Compute Using are set.

options.text: Drag the Rank item from the Analytics pane again
options.rationale: Rank is not an Analytics pane item.

explanation: Edit Table Calculation lets you change the type and the Compute Using setting, which gives the direction and the marks it runs across.

stem: Which field can have a quick table calculation applied directly?

options.text: `Minutes Watched` in the Data pane, not yet used in the view
options.rationale: The measure must be in the view first.

options.text: `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on the Rows shelf
options.rationale: Quick table calculations apply to measures in the view.

options.text: `Genre` on the Rows shelf
options.rationale: Genre is a dimension, so it has no quick table calculation menu.

options.text: `Plan Code` in the Data pane
options.rationale: A field outside the view cannot be given a quick table calculation.

explanation: You can only perform quick table calculations on measures in the view, since they compute over the marks that are drawn.

stem: Which two are quick table calculation types? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Percent difference
options.rationale: It is one of the listed types.

options.text: Median
options.rationale: Median is a reference line computation, not a quick table calculation.

options.text: Constant
options.rationale: Constant is a reference line value.

options.text: Create bins
options.rationale: Bins are created from the Data pane.

options.text: YTD total
options.rationale: It is one of the listed types.

explanation: The list includes Running total, Difference, Percent difference, Percent of total, Rank, Percentile, Moving average, YTD total, Compound growth rate, Year over year growth and YTD growth.

stem: Which two statements about quick table calculations are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: They compute over the marks already in the view
options.rationale: That is how table calculations work.

options.text: They add a new field with an equal sign to the Data pane
options.rationale: That describes a calculated field.

options.text: They are created with Analysis > Create Calculated Field
options.rationale: That menu creates calculated fields.

options.text: A delta symbol appears on the pill
options.rationale: The delta shows the calculation is applied.

options.text: They run on the underlying rows before the view is aggregated
options.rationale: They run after aggregation, over the marks in the view.

explanation: A quick table calculation is a menu choice on a measure already in the view, not a new field in the Data pane.

stem: How does an analyst create bins from the `Minutes Watched` measure?

options.text: Right-click the measure pill in the view and choose Quick Table Calculation > Bins
options.rationale: Quick table calculations do not include bins.

options.text: Drag Bins from the Analytics pane onto the view
options.rationale: The Analytics pane has no Bins item.

options.text: Select Analysis > Create Calculated Field and choose Bins
options.rationale: Bins have their own dialog and are not a formula type.

options.text: Right-click the measure in the Data pane and select Create > Bins
options.rationale: Bins are created from a measure in the Data pane.

explanation: Create > Bins opens a dialog where you enter the size of bins or let Tableau suggest one.

stem: An analyst selects `Minutes Watched` and picks histogram in Show Me. What aggregation does the measure on Rows use?

options.text: CNT (Count)
options.rationale: The aggregation changes from SUM to CNT because a histogram counts marks per bin.

options.text: SUM
options.rationale: SUM is the starting aggregation, but the histogram changes it.

options.text: AVG
options.rationale: Average is not what a histogram uses; it counts records.

options.text: MAX
options.rationale: Maximum would show only the largest value in each bin.

explanation: Tableau creates the bin field, puts it on Columns, moves the measure to Rows and changes its aggregation to count.

stem: Which two statements about bins are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Creating bins makes a new dimension
options.rationale: The binned field is a dimension named like `Minutes Watched (bin)`.

options.text: Creating bins makes a new measure
options.rationale: The result is a dimension.

options.text: The lower limit of each bin is inclusive
options.rationale: A value on the lower limit falls into that bin.

options.text: The upper limit of each bin is inclusive
options.rationale: It is the lower limit that is inclusive.

options.text: Binned fields can be used in calculations
options.rationale: Binned fields cannot be used in calculations.

explanation: Bins cut a continuous measure into equal ranges and create a dimension, the basis of a histogram.

stem: Which two statements describe building a histogram with Show Me? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The view must contain a single measure and no dimensions
options.rationale: That is when the histogram is available.

options.text: Tableau creates the bin field and puts it on Columns
options.rationale: The measure moves to Rows.

options.text: `Genre` has to be on Rows first
options.rationale: The view must contain no dimensions.

options.text: The measure on Rows keeps its SUM aggregation
options.rationale: It changes to CNT.

options.text: The analyst has to type a bin size
options.rationale: Tableau can suggest one.

explanation: The histogram option in Show Me needs one measure and no dimensions, and does the binning for you.

stem: Which setting in the Create Bins dialog controls how wide each range is?

options.text: Number of members
options.rationale: Bins are defined by their width, not by a member count.

options.text: Lower limit of bins
options.rationale: Each bin's lower limit is inclusive, but it follows from the size and is not the width setting.

options.text: Size of bins
options.rationale: It sets the width of every range, and Tableau can suggest a value.

options.text: Aggregation of bins
options.rationale: A bin field is a dimension of ranges, so no aggregation is chosen for it.

explanation: Bins cut a continuous measure into equal ranges. The Size of bins value sets the width of each range, and Tableau suggests one if the analyst does not enter their own.

stem: An analyst cannot create bins on a measure from a multidimensional (cube) data source. Which limitation explains this?

options.text: Bins only work with relational data sources
options.rationale: Bin creation is limited to relational sources.

options.text: Bins only work on date fields
options.rationale: Bins are created from a continuous measure, not only from dates.

options.text: Bins only work in Tableau Public
options.rationale: They are not limited to one edition of Tableau.

options.text: Bins only work on measures that have been aggregated
options.rationale: Bins are created from the measure in the Data pane, before any aggregation in a view.

explanation: The help for bins notes that they only work with relational data sources. Check the type of the data source first when the bin option is missing.

stem: Which two questions is a histogram of `Minutes Watched` per session suited to answer? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Do most sessions run short or long?
options.rationale: A histogram shows how values are distributed across the bins.

options.text: How many sessions fall into each range of minutes?
options.rationale: A histogram counts the marks in each bin.

options.text: How much has total viewing built up since January?
options.rationale: That is a running total over time, a quick table calculation.

options.text: Which plan is above its target value?
options.rationale: That needs a reference line on a chart by plan.

options.text: In what order should the plan tiers appear?
options.rationale: That is a sort, not a distribution.

explanation: A histogram counts the marks in each bin of a binned measure, so it shows the distribution of values. Running totals, targets and ordering are done with other tools.

stem: Which menu command opens the editor for a new formula-based field?

options.text: Map > Create Calculated Field
options.rationale: The Map menu is for map settings, and the command is on the Analysis menu.

options.text: Dashboard > Create Calculated Field
options.rationale: The Dashboard menu is for dashboard layout, and the command is on the Analysis menu.

options.text: Format > Create Calculated Field
options.rationale: Format controls how a view looks, and the command is on the Analysis menu.

options.text: Analysis > Create Calculated Field
options.rationale: This opens the calculation editor, where the field is named and its formula typed.

explanation: Calculated fields are created from the Analysis menu. After naming the field and typing the formula, the new field appears in the Data pane.

stem: How can an analyst tell in the Data pane that a field is a calculated field?

options.text: A delta symbol is shown on it
options.rationale: The delta marks a quick table calculation applied to a pill in the view.

options.text: An equal sign (=) is shown next to it
options.rationale: All calculated fields carry an equal sign in the Data pane.

options.text: It is listed under Parameters
options.rationale: Parameters live in their own section, apart from calculated fields.

options.text: It is always blue
options.rationale: Pill colour shows discrete or continuous, not whether a field is calculated.

explanation: A calculated field is marked with an equal sign in the Data pane. The delta symbol is for quick table calculations on pills in a view, which is a different thing.

stem: A Driftlight analyst needs a field holding only the first three characters of each `Subscriber ID`. Which formula does that?

options.text: `UPPER([Subscriber ID])`
options.rationale: UPPER changes the text to capital letters and keeps all of it.

options.text: `[Subscriber ID] / 3`
options.rationale: Division is arithmetic and does not cut a string.

options.text: `DATETRUNC('month', [Subscriber ID])`
options.rationale: DATETRUNC works on dates, and an ID is text.

options.text: `LEFT([Subscriber ID], 3)`
options.rationale: LEFT returns the given number of characters from the start of a string.

explanation: String functions such as `LEFT` and `UPPER` work on text. `LEFT` takes a part from the start of a string, while `UPPER` only changes its case.

stem: Which formula returns the number of days between a subscriber's `Signup Date` and `Cancel Date`?

options.text: `DATEDIFF('day', [Signup Date], [Cancel Date])`
options.rationale: DATEDIFF counts the date parts between two dates, here days.

options.text: `DATETRUNC('day', [Signup Date])`
options.rationale: DATETRUNC truncates one date to a level and returns a date, not a number of days.

options.text: `UPPER([Cancel Date])`
options.rationale: UPPER is a string function.

options.text: `LEFT([Signup Date], 3)`
options.rationale: LEFT is a string function and gives text.

explanation: Date functions work with date fields. `DATEDIFF` gives a number of days between two dates, which suits a "Days to Cancel" measure, while `DATETRUNC` returns a date.

stem: Which formula is an aggregate calculation rather than a row-level one?

options.text: `[Minutes Watched] / 60`
options.rationale: It is computed for every row and aggregated afterwards in the view.

options.text: `UPPER([Plan Code])`
options.rationale: A string function is computed row by row.

options.text: `SUM([Minutes Watched]) / COUNT([Session ID])`
options.rationale: It aggregates first and then divides, so it works at any level of detail.

options.text: `LEFT([Subscriber ID], 3)`
options.rationale: It is evaluated for each row.

explanation: A row-level calculation is computed for every row and then aggregated in the view. An aggregate calculation uses aggregate functions such as `SUM` and `COUNT` and divides the totals.

stem: An analyst wants the number of sessions in a calculated field. Which approach works?

options.text: Use `Sessions (Count)` in the formula
options.rationale: The (Count) field cannot be used in calculations.

options.text: Count an ID field, such as `COUNT([Session ID])`
options.rationale: A table's (Count) field cannot be used in calculations, so an ID field is counted instead.

options.text: Use `SUM([Sessions (Count)])`
options.rationale: Wrapping the field in an aggregation does not allow it in a calculation.

options.text: Drag `Sessions (Count)` into the formula as a parameter
options.rationale: Parameters hold a single value and do not supply counts.

explanation: The generated (Count) measure of a table is not available in calculations. Counting an ID field, such as `Session ID`, gives the same result inside a formula.

stem: Which two statements about calculated fields are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Tableau makes the field a measure when the formula returns a number
options.rationale: A numeric result gives a measure.

options.text: A quick table calculation is applied to them from the Analytics pane
options.rationale: Quick table calculations are applied from a measure pill's menu, not from the Analytics pane.

options.text: A formula can mix row-level values and aggregates, such as `[Minutes Watched] / COUNT([Session ID])`
options.rationale: Mixing the two in one formula is an error.

options.text: Right-clicking the field in the Data pane and choosing Edit changes its formula
options.rationale: Edit opens the calculation again.

options.text: They are created by dragging Reference Line into the view
options.rationale: A reference line draws a line and does not create a field.

explanation: A calculated field is a new field in the Data pane. It can be edited from its right-click menu and becomes a measure when it returns a number. Mixing a row-level value with an aggregate in one formula gives an error.

stem: Which two formulas are row-level calculations? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: `SUM([Minutes Watched]) / COUNT([Session ID])`
options.rationale: It aggregates before dividing, so it is an aggregate calculation.

options.text: `[Minutes Watched] / 60`
options.rationale: It is computed for every row, giving hours per session.

options.text: `COUNT([Session ID])`
options.rationale: COUNT is an aggregate function.

options.text: `[City] + ", " + [Country]`
options.rationale: String concatenation is evaluated for every row.

options.text: `SUM([Minutes Watched])`
options.rationale: SUM is an aggregate function.

explanation: Row-level calculations are computed for every row and aggregated later in the view. Formulas built on `SUM` or `COUNT` aggregate first and are aggregate calculations.

stem: Which description fits a parameter best?

options.text: A workbook variable that can replace a constant value in a calculation, filter or reference line
options.rationale: A parameter is one value, which the viewer can change.

options.text: A field that removes rows from the view based on its members
options.rationale: That describes a filter.

options.text: A formula that is computed for every row of a table
options.rationale: That describes a row-level calculated field.

options.text: A set of bins that groups a measure into ranges
options.rationale: That describes bins.

explanation: A parameter is a workbook variable, such as a number, date or string. It holds one value, which can stand in for a constant in a calculation, a filter or a reference line.

stem: Where does an analyst start to create a parameter?

options.text: From the Analytics pane by dragging Parameter into the view
options.rationale: The Analytics pane holds items such as Reference Line and Totals.

options.text: From a measure pill's menu, under Quick Table Calculation
options.rationale: That menu applies table calculations.

options.text: From the Filters shelf by choosing Add Parameter
options.rationale: The Filters shelf does not create parameters.

options.text: From the drop-down arrow at the top of the Data pane, choosing Create Parameter
options.rationale: That menu offers Create Parameter.

explanation: A parameter is created from the menu at the top of the Data pane. There the analyst chooses its data type and its allowable values.

stem: The head of content wants to switch every chart between minutes watched and number of sessions with one control. What should the analyst build?

options.text: A filter on `Minutes Watched`
options.rationale: A filter removes data by values and cannot swap one measure for another.

options.text: A manual sort of the measure pills
options.rationale: Sorting orders members and does not change the measure shown.

options.text: A parameter, used in a calculation that returns one measure or the other
options.rationale: A parameter holds the viewer's choice and the calculation reacts to it.

options.text: A reference line at the average
options.rationale: A line adds a value to the view and does not swap measures.

explanation: Swapping measures is the typical use of a parameter. The parameter provides the choice, and a calculation such as an IF test picks the measure to return.

stem: A viewer should be able to enter their own target and see a reference line move to it. What does the line need?

options.text: A quick table calculation of type Rank
options.rationale: Rank orders marks and gives no value to type in.

options.text: A parameter as its constant value
options.rationale: A parameter can replace the constant of a reference line.

options.text: A computed sort on the target field
options.rationale: A sort orders members and does not feed a line.

options.text: A bin field set to the target size
options.rationale: Bins group a measure into ranges, so they cannot be entered as a target.

explanation: A parameter can replace a constant in a reference line. After Show Parameter is chosen, viewers can type a value and the line follows.

stem: Viewers only need to choose which Genre members appear in a chart. Which is the simpler tool?

options.text: A parameter with a calculated field
options.rationale: It would also work but is more effort, since a parameter holds a single value.

options.text: A parameter with a reference line
options.rationale: A reference line does not decide which members show.

options.text: Totals set to Column Grand Totals
options.rationale: Totals add summary rows and do not select members.

options.text: A filter on `Genre`
options.rationale: Picking members of a field to show is what a filter is for.

explanation: Use a filter when viewers pick members of a field. Use a parameter when they supply a single value, such as a threshold, a target or the choice of a measure.

stem: Which two statements about parameters are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It can be used in any worksheet of the workbook
options.rationale: Parameters are global across the workbook.

options.text: It removes rows from the view as soon as it is created
options.rationale: A parameter does nothing until a calculation, filter or reference line uses it.

options.text: A string parameter does not support Range as its allowable values
options.rationale: Range is not available for string parameters.

options.text: Viewers can select several values of it at once
options.rationale: A parameter holds one value.

options.text: Its control is shown to viewers automatically
options.rationale: Show Parameter must be chosen.

explanation: A parameter is a single workbook-wide value. It has no effect until something uses it, and its allowable values can be All, List or Range, although a string parameter cannot use Range.

stem: Which three can use a parameter in place of a constant value? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: A calculation that swaps measures
options.rationale: A parameter can replace a constant in a calculation.

options.text: A Top N filter
options.rationale: The N can be picked by the viewer.

options.text: The connection to a data source
options.rationale: Connections are not values a parameter replaces.

options.text: A reference line
options.rationale: The line's value can be a parameter.

options.text: A bin's lower limit
options.rationale: Bin limits follow from the bin size and are not set by a parameter.

explanation: Parameters can replace a constant in a calculation, a filter such as Top N, or a reference line. The viewer chooses the value, and every part that uses it reacts.

stem: Which Analysis menu command sets the aggregation that totals use for all measures in a view?

options.text: Analysis > Totals > Total All Using
options.rationale: It lets the analyst pick one aggregation for every measure's total.

options.text: Analysis > Create Calculated Field
options.rationale: It opens the calculation editor and does not set a total.

options.text: Data > New Data Source
options.rationale: It connects to data and has nothing to do with totals.

options.text: Format > Totals
options.rationale: Format controls how a view looks, and the aggregation of totals is not set there.

explanation: Total All Using, under Analysis > Totals, picks the aggregation, such as Sum or Average, for all measures. For a single field the choice is made on the field itself.

stem: An analyst wants the total of one measure to use a different aggregation than the rest. What should they do?

options.text: Choose Analysis > Totals > Total All Using
options.rationale: Total All Using sets one aggregation for every measure's total, not for a single field.

options.text: Right-click the field in the view and select Total using
options.rationale: That sets the total aggregation for that field only.

options.text: Drag Totals again and drop it on Subtotals
options.rationale: That adds subtotals and does not change one field's aggregation.

options.text: Apply a quick table calculation of type Percent of total
options.rationale: That changes the measure into a percentage and does not set its total.

explanation: Total using, found on a field's right-click menu in the view, sets the aggregation of the total for that field. Total All Using does the same for all measures.

stem: A crosstab shows `SUM(Minutes Watched)` with Running total applied. What is true about adding totals?

options.text: Totals can be applied, but only as subtotals
options.rationale: The limit covers table calculations whatever the kind of total.

options.text: Totals can be applied once the pill is made discrete
options.rationale: Changing the pill type does not lift the limit.

options.text: Totals cannot be applied to table calculations
options.rationale: This is a stated limit of totals.

options.text: Totals are applied to the running total as long as the view has a header
options.rationale: A header is needed, but totals still cannot be applied to table calculations.

explanation: Totals need at least one header, and they cannot be applied to table calculations. A running total is a quick table calculation, so it gets no total.

stem: Which kind of field blocks grand totals when it is used in the view?

options.text: A continuous dimension
options.rationale: Grand totals cannot be applied to continuous dimensions.

options.text: A discrete dimension
options.rationale: Discrete dimensions give headers, which totals need.

options.text: A discrete measure
options.rationale: This is not one of the limits on grand totals.

options.text: A dimension on the Detail card
options.rationale: This is not one of the limits on grand totals.

explanation: A view needs at least one header for totals, and grand totals cannot be applied to continuous dimensions.

stem: Which two are limits on showing totals? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The view must have at least one header
options.rationale: Without a header there is nothing to attach a total to.

options.text: The view must contain only one measure
options.rationale: Totals can be shown for several measures.

options.text: Totals work only for discrete measures
options.rationale: This is not a stated limit.

options.text: Grand totals cannot be applied to continuous dimensions
options.rationale: This is a stated limit.

options.text: Totals require a Top N parameter
options.rationale: Parameters are unrelated to totals.

explanation: Totals need a header in the view and do not work for continuous dimensions. They cannot be applied to table calculations either.

stem: The Add Totals dialog offers drop targets when the analyst drags Totals from the Analytics pane. Which three are they? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Row Grand Totals
options.rationale: One of the three drop targets.

options.text: Pages
options.rationale: This is a shelf and not a totals target.

options.text: Subtotals
options.rationale: One of the three drop targets.

options.text: Detail
options.rationale: This is a card on Marks and not a totals target.

options.text: Column Grand Totals
options.rationale: One of the three drop targets.

options.text: Filters
options.rationale: This is a shelf and not a totals target.

explanation: Dragging Totals into the view opens the Add Totals dialog, where the analyst drops it on Subtotals, Row Grand Totals or Column Grand Totals.

stem: Which two ways display totals on a worksheet? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag Totals from the Analytics pane into the view
options.rationale: The Analytics pane holds Totals.

options.text: Right-click a measure pill and choose Quick Table Calculation > Totals
options.rationale: Quick table calculations do not include a Totals type.

options.text: Use the Analysis > Totals menu
options.rationale: The Analysis menu offers totals too.

options.text: Choose Create > Totals in the Data pane
options.rationale: Create offers fields such as bins, not totals.

options.text: Choose Edit Table Calculation on a pill
options.rationale: That changes how a table calculation is computed.

explanation: Totals come from the Analytics pane or from the Analysis > Totals menu. Quick table calculations and the Data pane's Create menu do not add them.

stem: The chart shows `Channel` sorted by subscriber count, ascending. The analyst wants the channel with the most subscribers at the top. What should they change?

options.text: Change Sort By to Alphabetic and the order to descending
options.rationale: This orders by channel name, so the channel at the top would be the last name alphabetically, not the largest.

options.text: Apply the Rank quick table calculation to the measure
options.rationale: Rank adds numbers to the marks and does not reorder the bars.

options.text: Add a Table-scope reference line at the maximum
options.rationale: A line marks a value on the axis and does not change the order of the members.

options.text: Switch the sort to descending
options.rationale: A computed sort follows the measure, and descending puts the largest value first.

explanation: The direction of a computed sort is part of the sort: one click on the sort icon gives descending, a second gives ascending. Switching the direction keeps the sort tied to the data.

stem: The `Plan` bars follow an order that matches neither their lengths nor the alphabet. Which kind of sort produces such a view?

options.text: A manual sort that places the plans in a chosen order
options.rationale: Only a manual order can put members in a sequence unrelated to their values or names, such as price tiers.

options.text: A computed sort by the subscriber count, descending
options.rationale: This would put the longest bar first, and the bars here are not in that order.

options.text: A computed sort by the subscriber count, ascending
options.rationale: This would put the shortest bar first, and the bars here are not in that order.

options.text: An alphabetic sort in either direction
options.rationale: Alphabetical order would give Basic, Basic with Ads, Premium, Standard or the reverse, which is not what the chart shows.

explanation: Computed sorts follow a value and alphabetic sorts follow names. When the sequence follows neither, such as plan tiers by price, the order was set by hand with a manual sort.

stem: `Genre` is sorted by `Titles (Count)`, descending, while the bars show `AVG(Runtime)`. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bars must get shorter down the chart, because a sort always uses the measure that is drawn
options.rationale: A computed sort can use any measure, not only the one on the axis.

options.text: The genres run from most titles to fewest, so the bars need not shorten
options.rationale: The sort field and the measure drawn are independent, so bar lengths can go up and down.

options.text: A sort by a field other than the one in the view is not allowed in Tableau
options.rationale: The Sort dialog lets you pick any field and an aggregation for the Field option.

options.text: The order is manual, because it does not follow the bar lengths
options.rationale: A sort by a field is computed even when it does not follow the bars you see.

explanation: Sort By > Field takes the field and aggregation that determine the order. That field can differ from the measure on the axis, which is why the bar lengths here do not run in order.

stem: The view has `Region` and then `Channel` on Rows, with the bars of `Subscribers (Count)` on Columns. The analyst clicks the sort icon on the measure axis. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It is a computed sort, so it follows the data when values change
options.rationale: Clicking a sort icon sorts by the measure, not by a hand-set order.

options.text: It sorts the regions themselves by their totals
options.rationale: Sorting from the axis orders the members inside each pane, not the panes.

options.text: It is a manual sort that copies the same order into every region
options.rationale: Manual sorts come from dragging headers or the Manual option.

options.text: It is a nested sort, so the channels are ordered within each region
options.rationale: Sorting from an axis gives a nested sort by default.

options.text: Sorting from the field label would nest too
options.rationale: Only sorting from an axis nests by default; a field label sort does not.

explanation: A sort from the axis is computed and nested: it orders the inner members within each pane, so panes can show different orders. Sorting from a field label does not nest.

stem: A bar chart shows minutes per genre. The analyst wants a line at the tallest bar of the whole chart. Which computation should the reference line use?

options.text: Minimum
options.rationale: Minimum would mark the shortest bar.

options.text: Maximum
options.rationale: Maximum draws the line at the largest mark.

options.text: Average
options.rationale: Average marks the mean of the bars, which sits below the tallest.

options.text: Total
options.rationale: Total sums all the marks and would sit far above any single bar.

explanation: A reference line computation is Total, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Average or Median. Maximum marks the largest mark in the scope.

stem: A line chart of daily minutes has a couple of extreme spikes. The analyst wants a reference line for the typical day that the spikes barely move. Which computation fits?

options.text: Average
options.rationale: The average is pulled up by extreme values, so the line would drift toward the spikes.

options.text: Maximum
options.rationale: Maximum marks the highest spike itself, not a typical day.

options.text: Total
options.rationale: Total sums every day and is not a typical value.

options.text: Median
options.rationale: The median is the middle value, so a few extreme days hardly move it.

explanation: Median draws the middle value of the marks. Average includes every value in its calculation, so a few extremes shift it.

stem: An analyst wants to shade the area within one standard deviation of the average on a continuous axis. Which item from the Add Reference Line dialog fits?

options.text: A distribution
options.rationale: Distributions are built from percentages, percentiles, quantiles or standard deviations.

options.text: A box plot
options.rationale: A box plot draws quartiles and whiskers, not a standard deviation range.

options.text: A reference line with the Median computation
options.rationale: A line marks one value and is not a shaded range.

options.text: A reference line with the Total computation
options.rationale: A line marks one summed value and does not shade a range.

explanation: The dialog builds reference lines, bands, distributions and box plots. A distribution is the one defined by percentages, percentiles, quantiles or standard deviations.

stem: Which three settings are part of the Add Reference Line dialog? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Size of bins
options.rationale: This is set when creating bins, not on a reference line.

options.text: Scope: Table, Pane or Cell
options.rationale: Scope sets how many lines are drawn.

options.text: Label: None, Value, Computation or Custom
options.rationale: The label setting chooses the text shown with the line.

options.text: Allowable values: All, List or Range
options.rationale: These belong to parameters.

options.text: Value: a constant or a computation
options.rationale: The value sets where the line is drawn, such as Constant or Average.

explanation: A reference line has a scope (Table, Pane or Cell), a value (a constant or a computation) and a label (None, Value, Computation or Custom).

stem: The analyst wants each month's `SUM(Minutes Watched)` shown as a percent change from the previous month. Which quick table calculation does that?

options.text: Difference
options.rationale: Difference gives the change in minutes, not as a percentage.

options.text: Percent of total
options.rationale: Percent of total gives each month's share of the whole.

options.text: Percent difference
options.rationale: It compares each mark with the previous one and expresses the change as a percentage.

options.text: Running total by month
options.rationale: Running total accumulates minutes month by month.

explanation: Difference shows the absolute change from the previous mark and Percent difference the relative change. Percent of total is a share and Running total is cumulative.

stem: A line of daily sessions jumps around from day to day. Which quick table calculation smooths the line by averaging neighbouring days?

options.text: Percentile
options.rationale: Percentile ranks each mark within the distribution and does not smooth.

options.text: Rank
options.rationale: Rank numbers the marks and does not smooth.

options.text: Moving average
options.rationale: It averages each mark with those around it, which smooths short-term swings.

options.text: Running total, by day
options.rationale: Running total accumulates and the line would only climb.

explanation: A moving average computes the average over a window of marks, so day-to-day spikes are damped.

stem: In Edit Table Calculation, what does the Compute Using setting decide?

options.text: The direction and marks the calculation runs across
options.rationale: Compute Using sets which way the calculation moves through the view's marks.

options.text: The field of the data source that gets aggregated
options.rationale: Aggregation is set on the pill, not through Compute Using.

options.text: The size of each bin in the view
options.rationale: Bin size is set in the Create Bins dialog.

options.text: Whether the field is treated as a dimension or measure
options.rationale: That is determined by the field itself and changed through the Data pane.

explanation: A table calculation computes over the marks in the view. Compute Using tells it in which direction and across which dimensions to run, which matters when the view has several.

stem: Which two Driftlight questions are answered with a quick table calculation? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Which genres lie above the content team's target?
options.rationale: That calls for a reference line.

options.text: What share of all viewing does each genre have?
options.rationale: Percent of total gives each mark's share.

options.text: In what order should the plan tiers appear?
options.rationale: That is a sort.

options.text: How many sessions fall into each range of minutes?
options.rationale: That is a histogram built from bins.

options.text: Which ten titles are highest by minutes?
options.rationale: Rank numbers the marks, so a top-ten table can be built on it.

explanation: Quick table calculations such as Percent of total and Rank compute over the marks in the view. Targets, ordering and distributions use other tools.

stem: A histogram uses bins of size 10 starting at 0. In which bin does a session of exactly 30 minutes fall?

options.text: The bin that ends at 30, because the upper limit is inclusive
options.rationale: The upper limit is not inclusive.

options.text: The bin that starts at 30, because the lower limit is inclusive
options.rationale: A value on the lower limit counts in that bin.

options.text: Both neighbouring bins, which each count it once
options.rationale: A record is counted in exactly one bin.

options.text: Neither, since values on a boundary are left out of the histogram
options.rationale: Boundary values are included, in the bin they start.

explanation: Each bin includes its lower limit and runs up to, but not including, the next one. So 30 belongs to the bin that starts at 30.

stem: An analyst halves the size of bins from 10 minutes to 5. What changes in the histogram?

options.text: There are fewer, wider bars, each covering a larger range
options.rationale: Wider bars would need a larger bin size.

options.text: The bars are the same but their aggregation changes to SUM
options.rationale: The size does not change the aggregation, which stays CNT.

options.text: The bin field turns into a measure
options.rationale: A bin field is a dimension whatever its size.

options.text: More, narrower bars, each covering a smaller range
options.rationale: Smaller bins cut the same range into more ranges.

explanation: The size of bins sets the width of each range. A smaller size gives more bars of narrower ranges, a larger size gives fewer, wider bars.

stem: An analyst tries to use `Minutes Watched (bin)` inside a calculated field. What is the limitation?

options.text: Binned fields can't be used in calculations
options.rationale: Tableau doesn't allow a bin field in a formula.

options.text: It works, but only inside an aggregate function such as COUNT
options.rationale: The limit applies whether or not an aggregate is used.

options.text: It works once the bin is converted to continuous
options.rationale: Changing the pill type does not lift the limit.

options.text: It works only when the data source is a cube
options.rationale: Bins themselves only work with relational sources, and the limit on calculations has nothing to do with cubes.

explanation: Creating bins gives a new dimension, but the help notes that binned fields can't be used in calculations. Use the original measure in the formula instead.

stem: Which two are ways to start a histogram of `Runtime`? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag Histogram from the Analytics pane into the view
options.rationale: The Analytics pane has no Histogram item.

options.text: Select the measure and pick histogram in Show Me
options.rationale: With one measure and no dimensions, Show Me can build it.

options.text: Right-click a `Genre` pill and choose Create > Bins
options.rationale: Bins are created from a measure, not from a dimension.

options.text: Right-click the measure in the Data pane, choose Create > Bins and use the bin field in the view
options.rationale: The bin field gives the ranges, and the measure is counted per bin.

options.text: Apply the Percentile quick table calculation to the measure
options.rationale: Percentile ranks marks and creates no bins.

explanation: A histogram needs a bin field. Show Me creates it for you, or you create it with Create > Bins and place it in the view.

stem: What does the formula `DATETRUNC('month', [Start])` return?

options.text: The number of months since the first session
options.rationale: Counting between dates is done by DATEDIFF.

options.text: The name of the month as text
options.rationale: A text result would need a function that formats the date as a string.

options.text: The number of sessions in that month
options.rationale: Counting sessions needs an aggregate such as COUNT.

options.text: A date, cut back to the month
options.rationale: DATETRUNC truncates a date to the given level and returns a date.

explanation: `DATETRUNC` keeps the date type, while `DATEDIFF` returns a number of date parts between two dates.

stem: Which two formulas return text? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: `DATEDIFF('day', [Signup Date], [Cancel Date])`
options.rationale: It returns a number of days.

options.text: `LEFT([Subscriber ID], 3)`
options.rationale: LEFT returns characters of a string.

options.text: `[Minutes Watched] / 60`
options.rationale: It returns a number.

options.text: `DATETRUNC('month', [Start])`
options.rationale: It returns a date.

options.text: `UPPER([Plan Code])`
options.rationale: UPPER returns a string in capital letters.

explanation: String functions such as `LEFT` and `UPPER` return text. Date functions return numbers or dates, and arithmetic returns numbers.

stem: The analyst created a parameter named Measure and showed it, but picking Sessions changes nothing in the chart. What is missing?

options.text: Range as the allowable values
options.rationale: The allowable values only define what can be chosen.

options.text: A calculation, filter or reference line using it
options.rationale: A parameter has no effect until something uses it.

options.text: A copy of the parameter on each worksheet
options.rationale: Parameters are global and work in any worksheet.

options.text: A quick table calculation on the measure
options.rationale: Table calculations do not read parameters automatically.

explanation: A parameter is only a stored value. To swap measures it has to feed a calculation, for example an IF test that returns one measure or the other, placed in the view.

stem: Which kind of value does a parameter hold?

options.text: Several members at once, as in a multi-select filter
options.rationale: A parameter holds one value, not a set of members.

options.text: A new value computed for every row of the data
options.rationale: That describes a row-level calculated field.

options.text: A single number, date or string chosen by the viewer
options.rationale: A parameter is one value of a given data type.

options.text: A set of rows picked by the viewer
options.rationale: Choosing rows to keep is what a filter does.

explanation: A parameter is a workbook variable such as a number, date or string. It holds one value that stays the same until the viewer changes it.

stem: Which two needs call for a filter rather than a parameter? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Show only the Mobile and TV sessions
options.rationale: Choosing members of a field to show is what a filter does.

options.text: Let the viewer swap between minutes and sessions
options.rationale: That is a parameter used in a calculation.

options.text: Let the viewer type a target value for a reference line
options.rationale: A single typed value is a parameter.

options.text: Let the viewer pick which genres appear in a chart
options.rationale: Picking members of `Genre` is a filter.

options.text: Let the viewer choose N for a top N titles table
options.rationale: N is one value, which a parameter supplies.

explanation: A filter removes data based on a field's members. A parameter supplies one value, such as a target, an N or the choice of a measure.

stem: A scatter plot has `AVG(Runtime)` on Columns and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows, with no discrete fields. Totals can't be added. Which requirement is not met?

options.text: The view must have at least one header
options.rationale: Totals attach to headers, and this view has none.

options.text: The view must contain a table calculation
options.rationale: Totals can't be applied to table calculations, so this is not a requirement.

options.text: The view must contain a continuous dimension
options.rationale: Grand totals can't be applied to continuous dimensions.

options.text: The view must be filtered by a parameter
options.rationale: Parameters have nothing to do with totals.

explanation: Totals need at least one header in the view. A view of two continuous measures has axes but no headers.

stem: A table lists `Country` within `Region`. The analyst wants a line that adds up each region's countries. Which drop target in the Add Totals dialog fits?

options.text: Row Grand Totals
options.rationale: Grand totals sum the whole table, not each region.

options.text: Column Grand Totals
options.rationale: Grand totals sum the whole table, not each region.

options.text: Filters
options.rationale: This is a shelf, not a drop target in the dialog.

options.text: Subtotals
options.rationale: Subtotals add up the inner members of each outer member, here the countries of a region.

explanation: Totals can be dropped on Subtotals, Row Grand Totals or Column Grand Totals. Subtotals sum within the outer header; grand totals cover the whole table.

stem: Which two items can be dragged from the Analytics pane into the view? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Totals
options.rationale: Totals are in the Analytics pane.

options.text: Create Parameter
options.rationale: Parameters are created from the Data pane's menu.

options.text: Bins
options.rationale: Bins are created from a measure in the Data pane.

options.text: Quick Table Calculation
options.rationale: Quick table calculations are applied from a pill's menu.

options.text: Reference Line
options.rationale: Reference Line is in the Analytics pane.

explanation: The Analytics pane holds items such as Totals and Reference Line. Parameters and bins are created from the Data pane, and quick table calculations from a pill's menu.

stem: The view has one reference line on the `SUM(Minutes Watched)` axis, with Scope set to Table and the value set to Average. What does the line mark?

options.text: The average of the genre bars, drawn once across the whole view
options.rationale: Table scope draws one line for the whole table, and Average is computed over the marks in the view.

options.text: Each genre’s average minutes per session, one line per bar
options.rationale: One line per bar would need Cell scope, and the computation runs over the marks, not over the sessions inside each bar.

options.text: The total minutes of every genre added together
options.rationale: That is the Total computation, not Average.

options.text: A shaded area between the shortest and the longest bar
options.rationale: Shading between two values is a reference band, not a line.

explanation: A reference line’s scope (Table, Pane or Cell) decides how many lines appear, and its value is a constant or a computation over the marks: Total, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Average or Median.

stem: This view draws one average line across both `Type` panes. The analyst wants a separate average line for Movie and for Series. Which two settings should the edited reference line have? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Scope: Pane
options.rationale: Pane scope draws one line per pane, so Movie and Series each get their own.

options.text: Value: Average, computed over the marks
options.rationale: The line should still be an average, now computed within each pane.

options.text: Scope: Table
options.rationale: Table scope is what the view has now: one line for everything.

options.text: Scope: Cell
options.rationale: Cell scope draws a line in every cell, here one per bar, not one per type.

options.text: Value: Constant
options.rationale: A constant is the same fixed number in every pane, not each pane’s own average.

options.text: Label: Custom
options.rationale: The label changes the text next to the line, not how many lines there are or where they sit.

explanation: Scope sets how many lines appear: one for the table, one per pane, or one per cell. With Type as the outer dimension on Rows, each type is a pane, so Pane scope with Average gives one average per type.

stem: The dashed line sits at exactly 500,000 minutes on every device’s axis, Driftlight’s target per device. How was it most likely added?

options.text: A reference line with the Average computation
options.rationale: An average line would sit at the mean of the bars, which moves with the data.

options.text: A reference line with a Constant value
options.rationale: A target that doesn’t depend on the data is a Constant reference line, optionally from a parameter.

options.text: A reference band from Minimum to Maximum
options.rationale: A band shades an area between two values; this is a single line.

options.text: A Running total quick table calculation
options.rationale: A table calculation changes the bars’ values; it doesn’t draw a line on the axis.

explanation: A reference line’s value is either a constant, such as a target (or a parameter), or a computation over the marks. A fixed target is a constant.

stem: The pill on Columns shows a delta symbol, and Comedy’s bar reads 24.4%. Which quick table calculation was applied to `SUM(Minutes Watched)`?

options.text: Running total
options.rationale: A running total adds up the bars one after another; it doesn’t give each genre a share.

options.text: Rank
options.rationale: Rank gives each bar a position number, not a percentage.

options.text: Percent of total
options.rationale: Percent of total divides each mark by the total of all marks, so each bar is a genre’s share.

options.text: Percent difference
options.rationale: Percent difference compares each mark with the one before it, not with the total.

explanation: A quick table calculation computes over the marks already in the view, and the delta on the pill marks it. Percent of total turns each genre’s minutes into its share of all minutes.

stem: The line of 2025 minutes climbs every month and never falls, because the measure has the Running total quick table calculation. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Each point adds that month’s minutes to the minutes of all earlier months
options.rationale: That is what a running total shows: cumulative viewing.

options.text: A delta symbol on the pill marks the table calculation
options.rationale: Tableau adds a delta to a field that has a quick table calculation.

options.text: The extract now stores cumulative minutes for each session
options.rationale: A table calculation works on the marks in the view; the data source is unchanged.

options.text: The same option is offered on dimension pills such as Device
options.rationale: Quick table calculations work only on measures in the view.

options.text: Removing the calculation leaves the line exactly as it is
options.rationale: Without it, each point shows only its own month’s minutes, which rise and fall.

explanation: A quick table calculation applies the most typical settings for its type to a measure in the view, and its result depends only on the marks shown. Running total accumulates them, so a line of minutes can only climb.

stem: The analyst right-clicks `Genre` on Rows to add a running total, but the menu has no Quick Table Calculation item. Why?

options.text: Quick table calculations can only be applied to measures in the view
options.rationale: Genre is a dimension; the calculation belongs on SUM(Minutes Watched).

options.text: Genre must be converted to continuous first
options.rationale: Converting a dimension to continuous doesn’t make it a measure to calculate on.

options.text: Running totals need a date field somewhere in the view
options.rationale: A running total can accumulate over any marks, such as bars of genres.

options.text: The data source must be an extract before table calculations work
options.rationale: Table calculations work on live connections and extracts alike.

explanation: "You can only perform quick table calculations on measures in the view." Right-click the measure pill, here SUM(Minutes Watched), and choose Quick Table Calculation.

stem: Each bar counts titles in a 30-minute range of `Runtime (bin)`. Into which bar does a title that runs exactly 60 minutes fall?

options.text: The bar labelled 30
options.rationale: That bin holds runtimes from 30 up to, but not including, 60.

options.text: The bar labelled 60
options.rationale: Bins are labelled by their lower limit, and the lower limit is inclusive, so 60 starts the 60 bin.

options.text: Both bars, because 60 sits on their shared edge
options.rationale: Every value falls into exactly one bin.

options.text: Neither: edge values go to a Null bin
options.rationale: Only missing values are Null; a runtime of 60 has a bin.

explanation: Bins cut a measure into equal ranges and create a new dimension. Each bin is named by its lower limit, and "the lower limit is inclusive".

stem: The analyst built this histogram by selecting only `Minutes Watched` and choosing histogram in Show Me. Which two things did Tableau do? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Created a new dimension, `Minutes Watched (bin)`, and put it on Columns
options.rationale: Show Me creates the bin field and places it on Columns.

options.text: Changed the measure on Rows from SUM to CNT (Count)
options.rationale: A histogram counts the marks in each bin, so the aggregation becomes a count.

options.text: Converted `Minutes Watched` to a string
options.rationale: The measure keeps its data type; a separate bin field is created.

options.text: Applied a Percent of total quick table calculation
options.rationale: A histogram counts; it doesn’t turn the counts into shares.

options.text: Created a set of the most common session lengths
options.rationale: Sets split members into In and Out; a histogram uses bins.

explanation: Histogram "is available in Show Me when the view contains a single measure and no dimensions". Tableau creates the bin field on Columns, moves the measure to Rows and "the aggregation changes from SUM to CNT (Count)".

stem: The analyst wants to use `Runtime (bin)` from this view in a calculated field that labels titles as short or long. What happens?

options.text: It works like any other dimension in the formula
options.rationale: Binned fields are the exception: they can’t be used in calculations.

options.text: It works, but only inside an aggregation such as ATTR
options.rationale: No aggregation makes a bin usable in a formula.

options.text: It works once the bin is converted to a measure
options.rationale: Converting doesn’t change the rule; bins can’t be used in calculations.

options.text: It can’t: binned fields can’t be used in calculations
options.rationale: The help says so; write the calculation on Runtime itself instead.

explanation: Bins only work with relational data sources, and binned fields can’t be used in calculations. A calculation on the measure (for example an IF on Runtime) is the way to label ranges.

stem: The calculated field `Hours` on Columns has the formula `[Minutes Watched] / 60`, and the pill reads `SUM(Hours)`. What kind of calculation is it?

options.text: An aggregate calculation, computed once per bar
options.rationale: An aggregate calculation aggregates inside the formula, as SUM([Minutes Watched]) / 60 would.

options.text: A row-level calculation: computed for every session, then summed in the view
options.rationale: The formula has no aggregation, so it runs per row, and the view aggregates the result.

options.text: A quick table calculation over the bars
options.rationale: A quick table calculation is set on a pill’s menu; this is a calculated field.

options.text: A string calculation, since the result is labelled Hours
options.rationale: The result is a number, so Tableau makes it a measure.

explanation: Row-level calculations, such as [Minutes Watched] / 60, are computed for every row and then aggregated in the view. Because it returns a number, Tableau makes it a measure with SUM.

stem: The bars show `Avg Minutes`, a calculated field with the formula `SUM([Minutes Watched]) / COUNT([Session ID])`. Which two statements are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It aggregates first and then divides, so it is right at any level of detail
options.rationale: That is an aggregate calculation: the ratio of the sums, per mark.

options.text: It returns a number, so Tableau makes it a measure
options.rationale: Calculated fields that return numbers become measures.

options.text: `[Minutes Watched] / COUNT([Session ID])` would give the same bars
options.rationale: Mixing a row-level field and an aggregate in one formula is an error.

options.text: `Sessions (Count)` could replace `COUNT([Session ID])` in the formula
options.rationale: A table’s (Count) field can’t be used in calculations; count an ID field.

options.text: It is computed for every session and then summed for each device
options.rationale: That describes a row-level calculation; this one aggregates inside the formula.

explanation: A ratio of aggregates, such as SUM(...) / COUNT(...), is an aggregate calculation: it aggregates first and gives the right value at any level of detail. Mixing aggregate and non-aggregate arguments is an error.

stem: `Plan Label` on Rows is a calculated field with the formula `UPPER([Plan Code])`. How does the Data pane mark it as a calculated field, and how do you change its formula?

options.text: A delta symbol next to it; choose Edit Table Calculation
options.rationale: The delta marks a table calculation on a pill, not a calculated field.

options.text: A paperclip icon next to it; choose Edit Group
options.rationale: The paperclip marks a group.

options.text: An equal sign next to it; right-click it and select Edit
options.rationale: "All calculated fields have equal signs (=) next to them in the Data pane", and Edit opens the formula.

options.text: A globe icon next to it; choose Geographic Role
options.rationale: The globe marks a field with a geographic role.

explanation: Calculated fields are created with Analysis > Create Calculated Field and show an equal sign in the Data pane. Right-click one and select Edit to change its formula.

stem: The line on this view is a constant target. Managers want to type their own target on the dashboard and see the line move. What does that need?

options.text: A parameter used as the line’s value, with its control shown
options.rationale: A parameter holds one value the viewer can change, and a reference line can use it in place of a constant.

options.text: A filter on Minutes Watched shown as a slider
options.rationale: A filter removes bars; it doesn’t move a line.

options.text: A set of the genres that reach the target
options.rationale: A set splits genres into In and Out; it doesn’t let the viewer type a value.

options.text: A Percent of total quick table calculation
options.rationale: Shares of the total don’t take a typed target.

explanation: "A parameter is a workbook variable such as a number, date, or string that can replace a constant value in a calculation, filter, or reference line." Show Parameter gives viewers the control.

stem: Which two requests for this view call for a parameter? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Let viewers switch the bars between minutes and number of sessions
options.rationale: Swapping measures takes a parameter used in a calculation.

options.text: Let viewers type a growth rate that a calculation applies to the minutes
options.rationale: A what-if rate is a single value the viewer supplies: a parameter.

options.text: Let viewers pick which genres appear
options.rationale: Picking members to show is a filter, which is simpler.

options.text: Combine two genres into one bar
options.rationale: Combining members is a group.

options.text: Show each genre’s share of all minutes
options.rationale: A share of the total is a quick table calculation.

explanation: Use a parameter when the viewer should supply a single value, such as a choice of measure, a threshold or a what-if rate, that parts of the workbook react to. To pick members of a field, a filter is simpler.

stem: The analyst created a parameter, `Target`, and chose Show Parameter. Changing the value in its control changes nothing in this view. Why?

options.text: Parameters only work on the sheet they were created on
options.rationale: Parameters are global across the workbook and can be used in any worksheet.

options.text: Its allowable values must be a List before the control works
options.rationale: All, List and Range all give working controls.

options.text: Nothing in the view uses the parameter yet
options.rationale: A parameter does nothing until a calculation, filter or reference line uses it.

options.text: It has to be dragged to the Filters shelf first
options.rationale: Parameters aren’t used by dropping them on Filters; something has to reference them.

explanation: "A parameter does nothing until something uses it." Use it in a calculation, a Top N filter or a reference line.

stem: The crosstab ends with a total row, where Movie reads 1,726,946 minutes. Which option added that row?

options.text: Row Grand Totals
options.rationale: Row grand totals add a total for each row, at the right, across the columns.

options.text: Column Grand Totals
options.rationale: Column grand totals total each column down the rows, giving a total row at the bottom.

options.text: Subtotals
options.rationale: Subtotals total within the outer headers; this view has one header per shelf.

options.text: A Total reference line
options.rationale: A reference line draws on an axis; this view is a text table.

explanation: Totals come from the Analytics pane (drop Totals on Subtotals, Row Grand Totals or Column Grand Totals) or Analysis > Totals. Column grand totals sum each column, here each type, over all devices.

stem: Which two statements about totals on a worksheet such as this one are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The view must have at least one header for totals
options.rationale: "The view must have at least one header."

options.text: Analysis > Totals > Total All Using sets the aggregation of the totals for all measures
options.rationale: Total All Using picks the aggregation the totals use.

options.text: Grand totals can be added for continuous dimensions
options.rationale: "Grand totals cannot be applied to continuous dimensions."

options.text: Totals can be applied to a quick table calculation
options.rationale: Totals can’t be applied to table calculations.

options.text: Totals can only be added from the Analytics pane
options.rationale: The Analysis > Totals menu offers them too.

explanation: Drag Totals from the Analytics pane or use Analysis > Totals. Total All Using chooses the aggregation for all measures; one field’s Total using is on its pill menu. A view needs a header, and continuous dimensions get no grand totals.

stem: The analyst opens Analysis > Totals to add Row Grand Totals to this line of monthly minutes, but no total appears. Why?

options.text: Totals need an extract of the data
options.rationale: Totals work on any connection.

options.text: Totals can only sum, and this measure is an average
options.rationale: The measure is SUM, and totals can use other aggregations too.

options.text: Totals need a filter on the date first
options.rationale: Filters don’t enable totals.

options.text: The view has no header, and grand totals can’t be applied to continuous dimensions
options.rationale: The months are a continuous axis, not headers, so there is nothing to total.

explanation: "The view must have at least one header", and "Grand totals cannot be applied to continuous dimensions." A continuous month axis has neither headers nor totals.
